h1: Training new sensory panellists in their first four weeks
title: Train sensory panellists in four weeks | Craft Beer School
desc: A four week plan for training new brewery sensory panellists: basic tastes, spiked off-flavours, triangle tests and checking who is ready.
teaser: A new panellist who has never smelt diacetyl on purpose is not a panellist yet. Four structured weeks fixes that.
standfirst: Most small breweries put new staff on the taste panel from day one and trust their opinions as much as anyone's. A four week training block gives them a shared vocabulary and gives you the data to decide when they are ready.
sections:
A taste panel is a measuring instrument. An untrained panellist is an uncalibrated one. They may be blind to diacetyl at three times its flavour threshold, or call every hoppy sample "skunky". Their votes still count, so they drag the panel's result toward noise.

The fix is not a long course. It is four weeks of short sessions, two or three per week of 20 to 30 minutes each, run before the main panel or at a fixed time each day. The aim is a panellist who can find the common faults, describe your own beers in agreed words and repeat their own answers.
Week one: basic tastes and attributes

Start with water solutions of the basic tastes: sugar for sweet, citric acid for sour, salt for salty and caffeine for bitter. Run them at two strengths and ask panellists to rank them. Some people struggle to tell sour from bitter. Better to learn that now.

Then move to beer. Taste your core range and a commercial pale lager. Agree on the words your brewery uses for each attribute and write them on one sheet. That sheet becomes the panel's dictionary.

This is the core of the training. Spike a clean, light lager with one off-flavour standard at a time. Commercial spiking kits exist for exactly this. Start with the faults most likely in your beer:

  • Diacetyl (butter, butterscotch). Flavour threshold in lager is often quoted at around 0.1 mg/l.
  • Acetaldehyde (green apple). Threshold around 10 mg/l.
  • Dimethyl sulphide (cooked sweetcorn). Threshold around 30 to 50 µg/l.
  • Oxidation (wet cardboard) and light strike (skunk).

Present each spike next to the unspiked base so the contrast is clear. Then repeat blind. Thresholds vary a lot from person to person, so write down who finds what. Our guide to running a sensory panel covers sample handling.
Week three: difference tests and the scale

Introduce triangle tests: three coded samples, two the same and one different, with the panellist asked to pick the odd one. Guessing gets one in three right, so you need repeated trials before you read anything into a score. Use spiked samples near threshold and real comparisons from your own production, such as two batches of the same beer.

This is also the week to teach your scoring scale. If your panel rates beers as true to brand or not, train it on reference samples so everyone agrees what a 3 and a 5 look like. Panellists drift toward the middle of a scale unless they practise using the ends.
Week four: check who is ready

Finish with a short validation round. Present a blind set: a few spiked samples, a few clean samples and one duplicate. A panellist is ready when they find the faults they were trained on at a reasonable rate, describe your beers in the panel's words and give the same answer to the duplicate both times.

Not everyone passes. Some people have a specific blind spot, for example to diacetyl. That person can still serve on the panel, with their diacetyl votes weighted less or set aside. Writing that down is better than pretending everyone tastes the same.
Run the sessions so the data is clean

How you run a session matters as much as what you serve. Taste mid-morning or mid-afternoon, not straight after lunch. Ask panellists to skip strong coffee, cigarettes and perfume for half an hour before. Serve samples of about 30 to 50 ml in identical clear or dark glasses with three digit codes, never the beer's name.

Keep the room quiet and stop people from discussing samples until everyone has written an answer. One confident voice saying "that is clearly buttery" can swing a whole table. Collect the sheets, then talk. In a brewpub with a hot back room, serve samples at a consistent temperature, around 10 to 12 °C, so warm samples do not suddenly reveal faults that cold ones hid.

Randomise the order of samples for each panellist. People tend to rate the first sample differently from the rest. Using the same order for everyone builds that bias into your results.
Keep the training going after week four

Training is not a one-off. Rerun a spiked set every month or two so skills do not fade. Keep a simple record of each panellist's hits and misses in a spreadsheet. Over a year that record tells you whose palate you trust for which fault. It also shows you when someone's results slip, which sometimes means a cold, sometimes means boredom.

The hard part is not the spiking. It is building the habit of tasting critically every day and recording it so the data means something.
Book the first session this week

Order a basic set of off-flavour standards, pick three people and put two 20 minute slots in the diary for next week. Start with sweet, sour and bitter in water. It costs almost nothing and it tells you on day one who on your team tastes what.
faqs: How long does it take to train a beer sensory panellist?
A basic block of about four weeks, with two or three short sessions a week, gets most people to a useful level. Skills keep improving with regular practice after that.
What off-flavours should new panellists learn first?
Start with the faults most likely in your own beer. For most breweries that means diacetyl, acetaldehyde, dimethyl sulphide, oxidation and light strike.
Three coded samples are presented, two identical and one different. The taster picks the odd one out. Random guessing is right one time in three, so repeated trials are needed.
Can someone with a blind spot still be on the panel?
Yes. Record the blind spot and give less weight to their votes on that specific fault while trusting them on others.
